Issued at 148 AM CDT Mon Jul 20 2026

Today and tonight:

Early morning water vapor imagery depicts a pair of upper- 
level short-wavelength troughs along the US/Canadian border with
the leading wave moving into southern Manitoba and the other 
crossing into southern Alberta. The leading wave is anchored by 
a seasonably strong 998 surface low pressure system moving into 
western Ontario, and is supporting a broad low-level jet across 
the Upper Mississippi River Valley as confirmed by some 30-40kt 
of flow sampled by the FSD VWP early this morning. Meanwhile, a 
surface high pressure system is centered directly over the Lower
Great Lakes early this morning leading to nearly calm winds and
clear skies. With surface temperatures dropping toward the 
lower 50s (locally upper 50s) early this morning, have been 
noting areas of patchy fog particularly near Lake Michigan and 
across the Kankakee River Valley. It is otherwise a quiet 
morning across our area. 

All eyes are on a cluster of storms moving into western 
Minnesota at press time. Per RAP-mesoanalyzed fields, the 
cluster of storms is located right on the eastern edge of an EML
plume centered on the northern US (00Z ARB RAOB sampled 800 to 
500mb lapse rates of around 8 K/km) and narrow surface-based 
instability plume that arcs from the southern US northward along
the South Dakota and Minnesota border. As westerly mid-level 
flow on the southern side of both upper-level waves continues to
advect the lapse rate plume eastward and southwesterly low- 
level flow facilitates low-level warm air advection into the 
Upper Mississippi River Valley, would have to think that the 
ongoing cluster of storms will intensify and/or new storms will 
develop near the Mississippi River in the coming hours. The 
resulting complex of storms should then dive southward along the
instability axis aligned with or just west of the Mississippi 
River through the morning reaching northern Iowa toward daybreak
and possibly northeastern Missouri by early afternoon (largely 
missing our area). 

Assuming this occurs, at least some airmass recovery may take 
place across eastern Iowa before new thunderstorms develop by 
mid-afternoon near the intersection of an approaching cold 
front (associated with the lead wave) and the residual outflow 
boundary from the early day MCS draped across central Iowa. Such
a result would squash any opportunity for the surface-based 
instability axis to shift into our area this afternoon, 
effectively eliminating the threat for severe weather in our 
area through the evening hours. Meanwhile, a separate regime of 
supercells could materialize closer to the surface cyclone in 
northern Wisconsin and Upper Michigan. The net result would be a
large gap in convective coverage across southern Wisconsin and 
northern Illinois this evening. 

Even with minimal coverage of storms this evening, could still 
envision a threat for a few thunderstorms overnight as the 
secondary upper-level waves slides overhead perhaps favoring the
10 PM through 6 AM window. With instability profiles largely 
being forced by the eastern edge of a worked-over lapse rate 
plume (perhaps 1000-1500 J/kg of MUCAPE) but otherwise stellar 
shear profiles (effectively 45-55 kt in the elevated convective 
layer), would still need to watch for a storm to become severe 
with a threat for damaging winds or damaging hail. However, 
coverage of severe weather would largely be consistent with a 
Level 1 out of 5 threat level in our area and indeed on an 
isolated basis. (Oftentimes, the HRDPS performs well with 
summertime convective regimes and has consistently shown this 
forecast outcome for every run). 

Now, if the cluster of storms in western Minnesota croaks and 
new development in western Wisconsin is kept to a minimum this 
morning, the surface-based instability axis would have a much 
better opportunity to arc northeastward into northern Illinois 
and southern Wisconsin this evening. Thus would set the stage 
for a more concerning severe weather scenario locally where the 
overlap of intense almost cool-season like kinematics with warm-
season instability profiles would support explosive supercell 
development and subsequent growth into bowing clusters of storms
with a threat for all hazards across our area. At this point, 
do not think this scenario is particularly likely given trends 
in western Minnesota (a Severe Thunderstorm warning was
recently issued for the cluster confirming it is intensifying).

When taken altogether, will cautiously advertise a largely dry 
day with highs in the mid 80s. Then, will feature mid-range 
chance (40-50%) PoPs during the overnight hours for isolated to
scattered storms. Needless to say, will be watching upstream 
trends closely in case the ship needs to turn to feature higher 
chances for storms later today.
